enhanced.fullText:
The Occupational Safety and Health Act of 1970, codified at 29 U.S.C. §§ 651-678, establishes comprehensive workplace safety standards that apply to virtually all higher education institutions as employers. The Act created the Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) within the Department of Labor, empowering it to promulgate and enforce workplace safety regulations under 29 CFR Parts 1900-1999.

Higher education institutions must comply with OSHA's general duty clause under 29 U.S.C. § 654(a)(1), which requires employers to provide workplaces "free from recognized hazards" that could cause death or serious physical harm. This encompasses laboratories, research facilities, maintenance operations, dining services, and all campus workplaces where employees are present.

Key compliance obligations include mandatory safety training programs under 29 CFR § 1926.95 for construction activities and 29 CFR § 1910.1450 for laboratory operations. Universities must establish written hazard communication programs per 29 CFR § 1910.1200, including Safety Data Sheet management and chemical labeling protocols. Research institutions face additional requirements under 29 CFR § 1910.1450 (Laboratory Standard), mandating Chemical Hygiene Plans and designated Chemical Hygiene Officers.

Injury and illness recordkeeping requirements under 29 CFR Part 1904 mandate maintenance of OSHA Form 300 logs for workplaces with 11+ employees, with annual summaries posted from February 1-April 30. Severe injuries requiring hospitalization, amputations, or fatalities must be reported to OSHA within 8-24 hours under 29 U.S.C. § 657(c)(2).

Enforcement mechanisms include workplace inspections, citations, and monetary penalties. Under 29 U.S.C. § 666, willful or repeated violations can result in penalties up to $156,259 per violation, while serious violations carry penalties up to $15,625 each. Universities cannot retaliate against employees who report safety concerns under 29 U.S.C. § 660(c).

Recent updates include increased penalty amounts under the Federal Civil Penalties Inflation Adjustment Act and enhanced reporting requirements for severe injuries. State-plan states may impose additional requirements beyond federal OSHA standards, requiring institutions to monitor both federal and state-specific obligations for comprehensive compliance.
enhanced.summary: OSHA requires higher education institutions to maintain safe workplaces, provide employee safety training, implement hazard communication programs, maintain injury/illness records, and report severe incidents to federal authorities.
enhanced.requirements:
## Workplace Safety Programs
- Establish comprehensive safety programs covering all campus operations
- Implement written hazard communication programs per 29 CFR § 1910.1200
- Develop Chemical Hygiene Plans for laboratory operations under 29 CFR § 1910.1450
- Provide mandatory safety training for employees in hazardous work areas

## Recordkeeping and Documentation
- Maintain OSHA Form 300 injury/illness logs for establishments with 11+ employees
- Post annual summary of injuries from February 1 - April 30
- Preserve safety training records and inspection documentation
- Keep Safety Data Sheets readily accessible to employees

## Incident Reporting
- Report fatalities to OSHA within 8 hours of occurrence
- Report severe injuries requiring hospitalization within 24 hours
- Document all workplace incidents and corrective actions taken

## Personal Protective Equipment
- Assess workplace hazards and provide appropriate PPE at no cost to employees
- Train employees on proper PPE selection, use, and maintenance
- Establish PPE inspection and replacement protocols
enhanced.reportingRequirements: Annual Form 300A summary posting required February 1-April 30. Fatalities must be reported within 8 hours, severe injuries within 24 hours to nearest OSHA office. Quarterly electronic submission required for establishments with 250+ employees.
